Course Description

Modern AI depends on systems that move data, run tensor operations, manage memory, and coordinate processors. In this course you predict their costs, build key pieces, and measure where the time goes.

There are four modules: large-scale data processing (Weeks 1–4, Christopher Jermaine), then distributed and parallel computing (Weeks 5–8), distributed computing for tensors and ML (Weeks 9–11), and GPU hardware (Weeks 12–14), taught by Yuke Wang.

Who This Course Is For

This course is for juniors in AI, CS, math, or statistics who are stronger in math and ML than in systems programming.

Prerequisites (proposed; the current catalog lists COMP 215, 222, and 345): COMP 345 and one of CMOR 302, CMOR 303, MATH 221, MATH 354, or MATH 355. You should also know Python at the level of COMP 182.

Not required: prior GPU programming, PyTorch, computer architecture, or cluster experience. These foundations are taught in the course.

Before class starts: a four-hour self-paced primer on Python, NumPy, the terminal, and git, with a short math and ML self-check.

Learning Objectives

By the end of the course, you will be able to:

  • Model data as relations and query it with relational algebra, relational calculus, and SQL.
  • Clean, deduplicate, tokenize, and shard a large text corpus in parallel with Spark, respecting licensing and privacy.
  • Explain processes, threads, and network costs; write message-passing and collective programs; model communication cost.
  • Compare data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism and state sharding; analyze distributed matrix multiplication; design a 3D layout under a memory budget.
  • Explain GPU execution, the memory hierarchy, and number formats; write a Triton kernel and analyze it with the roofline model.
  • Explain where time goes when PyTorch runs a model (kernel launches, operator dispatch, and graph compilation) and compare eager and compiled execution.
  • Predict, measure, and explain memory, throughput, scaling efficiency, and energy, using traces to justify a systems change.

The System You Will Study and Build

Six assignments build one pipeline, from a raw Wikipedia dump to a trained model. The diagram shows each stage and what it reads and writes; the pipeline section of the course website shows each stage’s data format, shape, and a real example. Staff provide the model, autograd, optimizer, and reference programs; you build selected components, test them, and explain their performance.

D3's shards follow a written dataset contract, which T1 and T3 read. T2 uses synthetic tensors to isolate communication. If one of your earlier stages is incomplete, start the next from the staff reference output.

How the Course Works

Each week

  • Two lectures each week, except during university closures. Each lecture comes with a runnable notebook.
  • One recitation: hands-on help with tools, starter code, and math.
  • One concept check: a short quiz with unlimited attempts, graded for completion.
  • Office hours with instructors and TAs.

Each assignment: predict, build, measure

  • Predict the cost first: bytes, FLOPs, memory, and time.
  • Implement the assigned component with starter code and public tests. A checkpoint checks correctness on small inputs before the deadline.
  • Measure at scale and explain any gap from your prediction, using traces to test your explanation.

Reading the schedule

Each lecture in the schedule lists its topics. BUILD marks what you implement; STRETCH is optional.

Software and Computing

  • Tools. Python, PySpark, and Parquet for data; mpi4py, torch.distributed (NCCL), PyTorch, and Triton for training systems. Required code is Python and Triton.
  • Provided. Tested package versions, a job launcher, the model and optimizer, reference implementations, and bounded CPU and GPU configurations.
  • Scope. You write selected kernels, communication logic, and experiments, not a whole framework. Full 3D training is optional; its layout and cost analysis are required.
  • Compute. Every graded run fits a guaranteed per-student allocation. Bigger runs are optional. If the cluster goes down near a deadline, the deadline moves.

Data (D)

Training (T)

D1 Collect

Due Week 3

What you build: Stream-parse a Wikipedia dump into Parquet; an approved library strips wikitext markup.

Scaling study: Throughput vs. worker count; find the bottleneck; estimate full-dump time and cost.

T1 GPU and framework execution

Due Week 14

What you build: Write a Triton reduction or fused elementwise kernel, check it against PyTorch, and use it in the forward pass of a supplied model on your D3 data; compare eager, kernel, and compiled execution. Checkpoint: correct kernel and timing harness.

Scaling study: Predict memory traffic and arithmetic intensity; separate compile, launch, and steady-state costs; explain the bottleneck with a trace.

D2 Process

Due Week 5 (Wed, before recess)

What you build: Normalize the corpus and compute statistics with Spark DataFrames and SQL; tests compare your output with a single-machine run.

Scaling study: Strong and weak scaling; effect of partition count.

T2 Distributed programming

Due Week 10

What you build: Write a CPU ring all-reduce with mpi4py point-to-point messages and a torch.distributed/NCCL benchmark, including a guided two-server run. Checkpoint: correct collectives on small tensors.

Scaling study: Vary message size, rank count, and topology; fit latency and bandwidth and compare predictions with measurements.

D3 Build the dataset

Due Week 7

What you build: Deduplicate with MinHash and LSH in Spark (the checkpoint), train a BPE tokenizer with the provided trainer, and write shards that pass the contract checker. Stretch: write BPE training yourself.

Scaling study: Dedup cost vs. corpus size; LSH accuracy vs. time; tokens per second.

T3 Parallel training systems

Due Week 12

What you build: Implement data-parallel gradient averaging, check one update against a single-process reference and PyTorch DDP, and train on D3 data. Guided tensor- and pipeline-parallel exercises; analyze a 3D layout with a supplied simulator. Checkpoint: correct DP update and layout tests.

Scaling study: Compare replicated and sharded state, communication volume, and pipeline bubbles; justify a layout under a fixed GPU and memory budget.

Exams (30%)

The midterm in Week 8 covers Weeks 1–7: data processing and the first weeks of distributed computing. The final is cumulative, emphasizing Weeks 8–14 and the connections between the modules. Both test reasoning, not memorization. Practice exams are provided, and you may bring one page of notes.

Getting Help

  • Fell behind? Start the next stage from the reference output.
  • Missed a checkpoint? A TA will contact you.
  • Stuck on tools? Come to recitation or office hours.
  • Need time? Use slip days.
  • New term? See the glossary.
  • Extra help: Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 3, for MinHash and LSH; the PyTorch and NCCL documentation listed below for framework and distributed execution.

Course Policies

Late work

You have five slip days per semester, with at most two per submission. Reference outputs come out 48 hours after each deadline, and no submissions are accepted after that. Accommodations and outages are handled separately.

Collaboration

Discuss ideas freely. Write your own code and analysis. Provided code and reference outputs may be used. Don’t share or view others’ code. Every assignment, including T3, is individual.

AI tools

You may use AI to explain concepts, read documentation, and debug. You may not use it to write the parts each handout lists as yours, such as Spark jobs in D2/D3, the kernel and measurement code in T1, collective logic in T2, or gradient synchronization in T3. Cite any AI use, including your prompts.

Code check-offs

After D3 and T3, you do a ten-minute individual code walkthrough with staff. The handout lists the questions, the criteria, and how much the check-off counts toward that assignment.

Shared resources

Test at small scale first, and release resources when you finish. Idle jobs count against your allocation.

Honor Code

The Rice Honor Code applies. See honor.rice.edu.

Accommodations

Register with the Disability Resource Center, then talk with an instructor early in the semester.

Selected Readings

There is no textbook. Handouts list the readings and tested software versions.

Large-scale data processing (Weeks 1–4)

  • Codd, “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks,” CACM 1970.
  • Dean and Ghemawat, “MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters,” OSDI 2004.
  • Zaharia et al., “Resilient Distributed Datasets: A Fault-Tolerant Abstraction for In-Memory Cluster Computing,” NSDI 2012.
  • Armbrust et al., “Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark,” SIGMOD 2015.
  • Leskovec, Rajaraman, and Ullman, Mining of Massive Datasets, Chapter 3.
  • Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, “Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units,” ACL 2016.
  • Lee et al., “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better,” ACL 2022.
  • Penedo et al., “The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale,” NeurIPS 2024 (Datasets and Benchmarks).

Distributed, ML, and GPU systems (Weeks 5–14)

  • NVIDIA, CUDA Programming Guide: execution hierarchy, GPU memory, synchronization, and streams. CUDA guide
  • PyTorch documentation: tensors, operator dispatch, torch.compile, torch.func (vmap), and asynchronous CUDA execution. PyTorch dispatch · Compilation · torch.func
  • Williams, Waterman, and Patterson, “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures,” CACM 2009.
  • Tillet, Kung, and Cox, “Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations,” MAPL 2019.
  • NVIDIA, NCCL User Guide: collectives, process and device mapping, ordering, and synchronization. PyTorch Distributed Overview: communication primitives and parallel execution. NCCL ordering · Distributed overview
  • Narayanan et al., “Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM,” SC 2021: composing data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. Paper
  • Rajbhandari et al., “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models,” SC 2020.
  • Bengio et al., “A Neural Probabilistic Language Model,” JMLR 2003, for the supplied workload.
  • Thakur, Rabenseifner, and Gropp, “Optimization of Collective Communication Operations in MPICH,” IJHPCA 2005, for collective cost models.
  • van de Geijn and Watts, “SUMMA: Scalable Universal Matrix Multiplication Algorithm,” Concurrency: Practice and Experience 1997, for 2D matrix multiplication.
  • Agarwal et al., “A Three-Dimensional Approach to Parallel Matrix Multiplication,” IBM Journal of Research and Development 1995, for 3D matrix multiplication.

Glossary

Term

Meaning

Partition

A slice of a dataset handled by one worker.

Shuffle

Moving data between workers by key, over the network.

Data skew

Uneven partitions, so a few workers do most of the work.

MinHash and LSH

Hashing tricks that find similar documents without comparing every pair.

BPE

Byte-pair encoding: a tokenizer that repeatedly merges the most common pair of symbols.

Shard

One file of a dataset split across many files.

Dataset contract

The written format that D3 produces and T1 and T3 read.

FLOP

One floating-point operation (an add or a multiply).

Arithmetic intensity

FLOPs per byte moved to or from memory.

Roofline model

Attainable speed ≤ min(peak compute, bandwidth × arithmetic intensity).

Kernel

A function that runs on the GPU across many threads.

HBM

The GPU’s main memory: large but slower than on-chip memory.

Tile

A small block of a matrix kept in fast memory and reused.

Collective

A communication step that involves every GPU in a group.

All-reduce

Every GPU sends a vector and receives the sum. It equals a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather.

Reduce-scatter

Every GPU sends a vector and receives one slice of the sum.

All-gather

Every GPU sends one slice and receives all slices.

α–β model

Sending n bytes takes about α + nβ: α is the latency and β the time per byte (1 ÷ bandwidth). From Week 7, lectures write the same model as α + n/β, with β the bandwidth.

Data parallelism

Partition examples across workers and synchronize gradients; the model is replicated, though its state may also be sharded.

Tensor parallelism

Partition tensors and operations within a layer across devices, communicating partial results or inputs as needed.

ZeRO

Data parallelism that splits optimizer state (and optionally more) across GPUs.

MFU

Model FLOP/s achieved ÷ peak FLOP/s of all GPUs used, at the stated precision.

Strong and weak scaling

Strong: fixed problem, more workers. Weak: problem grows with workers.

SIMT

Single instruction, multiple threads: GPU threads execute in groups, with costs from divergent paths and memory access patterns.

Autograd

Automatic differentiation that tracks operations and computes gradients; its saved intermediates and execution affect memory and runtime.

Operator dispatch

Selecting the implementation of an operation for its tensor properties and execution backend.

Graph compilation

Transforming captured operations into executable code; compilation and graph breaks affect performance.

Rank and process group

A rank identifies a process within a group whose members participate in communication.

NCCL

NVIDIA library providing GPU communication primitives, including collectives, within and across servers.

Pipeline parallelism

Partition layers into stages; pass microbatches between stages, balancing work and idle pipeline bubbles.

3D parallelism

Compose data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism. In a simple rectangular layout, GPU count is DP × TP × PP.

FSDP

Fully sharded data parallelism: shard model state across data-parallel workers and communicate it when needed.
